UNITED STATES OF AMERICA
                                 BEFORE THE
                   FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION



PJM Interconnection, L.L.C.                          )                Docket No. ER26-3380-000



                  MOTION FOR LEAVE TO ANSWER AND ANSWER OF
                   THE NEW JERSEY BOARD OF PUBLIC UTILITIES


         On July 31, 2026, PJM Interconnection, L.L.C. (“PJM”) proposed revisions to the

Reliability Assurance Agreement Among Load Serving Entities (“RAA”) and the Open Access

Transmission Tariff (“Tariff”) to establish the Reliability Backstop Procurement (“RBP”). On

August 21, 2026, the New Jersey Board of Public Utilities (“Board”) submitted comments. 1

         On September 10, 2026, PJM filed a Motion for Leave to Answer and Answer. 2 Pursuant

to Rules 212 and 213 of the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission’s (“Commission” or “FERC”)

Rules of Practice and Procedure, the Board respectfully moves for leave to answer and submits

this Answer to provide additional information and context that will assist the Commission in its

decision-making process.

    I.   Motion for Leave to Answer

         While Rule 213(a)(2) generally prohibits answers to protests and comments, good cause

justifies the Commission’s granting this motion and accepting this Answer because it provides




1
 PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., Comments of the New Jersey Board of Public Utilities, Docket No. ER26-
3380 (Aug. 21, 2026) (“NJ BPU Comments”).
2
 PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., Motion for Leave to Answer and Answer of PJM Interconnection, L.L.C.,

                                                 1
 useful and relevant information that will assist the Commission in its decision-making process. 3

The information presented here came to the Board’s attention recently, during its efforts earlier

this month to review Load Adjustments in New Jersey and compare those Load Adjustments to

the proposed RBP cost obligations. 4

    II.   Answer

          PJM has proposed to use the 6.8 GW shortfall from the 2028/2029 Base Residual Auction

(“BRA”) as the initial target amount for the RBP. 5 As stated in its Comments to PJM’s RBP

Proposal, the Board ultimately supports PJM using this value for setting the procurement target;

the Board understands that aligning this target more directly with distinct large loads would require

additional time, and the Board understands the importance of running this backstop procurement

promptly.6

          The Board submits this Answer to express concern over the inputs used to establish PJM’s

cost allocation proportions set forth in its RBP Proposal. As explained in PJM’s Answer, the

proposed RBP cost allocations are based on the Load Adjustments between 2026 and 2028 that the

electric distribution companies (“EDCs”) submitted to PJM.7 Conceptually, the Board supports

145 FERC ¶ 61,035, at P 32 (2013); Wis. Pub. Serv. Corp., 144 FERC ¶ 61,093, at P 27 (2013); Iberdrola
Renewables, Inc. v. Bonneville Power Admin., 137 FERC ¶ 61,185, at P 17 (2011); SW Power Pool, Inc.,
119 FERC ¶ 61,199 at P 18 (2007); and Allegheny Elec. Coop. v. PJM Interconnection, 119 FERC ¶
61,165 at P 10 (2007).
4
 A recent revision to PJM Manual 19, effective June 30, 2026, added a new step in the Load Forecast
Adjustment process requiring submitters to provide their Relevant Electric Retail Regulatory Authority
(“RERRA”) with an opportunity to review their adjustments. See Revision 39 to PJM Manual 19,
Attachment B.
5
 See PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., Reliability Backstop Procurement to Address Resource Adequacy
Concerns Stemming from Large Loads, Docket No. ER26-3380 (July 31, 2026) (“PJM RBP Proposal”),
Transmittal Letter at 31.
6
    NJ BPU Comments at 4.
7

                                                   2
 this approach because “[e]ach [EDC] zone/area’s proportional share of the total Load Adjustment

MW is a means of capturing the zone/area’s proportional share of the influx of new large load that

is projected to come online in the near future.” 8 However, the Board is concerned that substantial

discrepancies exist in the inputs each EDC zone/area used to develop the Load Adjustment, and

that these discrepancies will result in a discriminatory cost allocation outcome.             Undue

discrimination occurs when entities are “similarly situated,” and there is “no legitimate reason for

the difference in treatment.” 9        Here, different EDC zones/areas may obtain different cost

allocations due to differences in the assumptions and inputs used in forming their 2026 Load

Adjustments, rather than differences in actual load growth alone. This inconsistent set of

assumptions does not provide a legitimate reason for different treatment when establishing cost

allocations.

           To this end, the Board recommends that PJM run the backstop as proposed starting in

September 2026, 10 and requests that FERC require PJM to submit a compliance filing to reform

its cost-allocation methodology using updated Load Adjustments. Specifically, the Board requests

that this reformed methodology establish a consistent MW threshold (50 MW) for large loads

reported across each zone/area so the Load Adjustments used for cost allocation in the RBP can

appropriately capture each zone/area’s proportional share of large load growth.

      i.         Inconsistencies in Large Load MW Thresholds Across Zones/Areas Result in a Cost

                 Allocation Result that is Discriminatory




8
    Id. at 72.
9
 PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., 184 FERC ¶ 61,087, P 46 (2023) (citing Mo. River Energy Servs. v. FERC,
918 F.3d 954, 958 (D.C. Cir. 2019)).
10

           Board Staff recently met with the EDCs under its retail jurisdiction to discuss the 2027

Load Adjustments. This is a new process established under recent revisions to PJM Manual 19.11

The Board used this process to better understand the Load Adjustment process. It is now clear that

the 2026 Load Adjustments used to determine PJM’s proposed cost allocation methodology 12

relied on data from EDCs with substantially different characteristics across the PJM footprint.13

For example, the Board understands that, in New Jersey, while some EDCs reported load growth

only for new large loads of 50 MW and above, other EDCs reported all Load Adjustments with no

specific MW threshold. Importantly, PJM used these inputs in its Load Adjustment, which

determines RBP cost allocation.

          Presentations from PJM’s September 2025 Load Analysis Subcommittee suggest these

inconsistencies could be regional, with the result being that EDCs receive different RBP cost

allocations based not on load growth alone but on the characteristics they chose to include as Load

Adjustments at the time. For example, FirstEnergy’s presentation states it uses loads 50 MW or

greater as inputs to the Large Load Adjustment, 14 while Duke Energy states that it reported

expansions of 20 MW or greater 15 – note, PJM later removed Duke Energy’s Load Adjustment

 because PJM determined its economic models would capture the load growth. 16 It is unclear how

pervasive these different treatments were because the EDC zones/areas providing Load

Adjustments generally did not specify whether they used a MW threshold. Therefore, the Board

thinks allocating costs using these inputs is unduly discriminatory because some loads that are less

than 50 MW in one zone may need to take on RBP obligations, whereas loads of the same size in

a different zone will not, solely because its EDC zone/area decided to include it or not in its Large

Load Adjustment.

       Importantly, PJM’s original goals for the Large Load Adjustment process were to enhance

transparency, improve accuracy, and mitigate double counting, 17 and, for this reason, it may not

have been necessary for each EDC to use consistent methods during this initial reporting period.

However, if PJM’s RBP Proposal is approved, these inputs will result in substantial RBP cost

obligations for zones/areas and therefore, the Board thinks it is crucial to revisit these inputs to

establish a consistent threshold and treatment.

       Ultimately, the Board supports PJM’s use of Large Load Adjustments to determine RBP

cost allocation because it is roughly commensurate with large load growth in zones/areas and these

customers have contributed most to PJM’s resource adequacy shortfall. However, the Board thinks

this element of the RBP must be revised so that zones/areas receive consistent treatment in the

RBP. The Board thinks this issue can be resolved after the RBP is held but before the RBP cost

 apportionment and thinks that PJM should file a compliance filing that uses a consistent threshold

across zones/areas in the Load Adjustment. 18

III.    Conclusion

        The Board recently became aware of these significant reporting inconsistencies and

appreciates FERC’s consideration of the Board’s Answer. The Board thinks these changes can be

made without necessitating substantial reform of PJM’s underlying RBP Proposal.



Respectfully,

Commission’s discretion to order a compliance filing revising tariff provisions meant to rectify
inconsistencies with proposal’s intent.).
